Bigeye sculpin (Triglops nybelini) is a small-bodied marine cottid found in Arctic and subarctic waters, where individuals exhibit a maximum recorded total length of 14.5 centimeters [Li = 14.5 centimeters]. Detailed growth analyses indicate that the onset of gonadal development occurs at a distinctly smaller body size, with puberty observed when fish attain a total length of 5.6 centimeters [Lp = 5.6 centimeters]. This substantial size differential between the length at maturity and the ultimate length suggests a prolonged period of somatic growth following reproductive activation, a pattern common among slow-growing cold-water teleosts. Morphometric data from field-collected specimens have been used to estimate body mass from length, revealing that adult males achieve an ultimate wet weight of approximately 45.9 grams [Wwi = approximately 45.9 grams]. Reproductively active females, by contrast, reach a wet weight at puberty of about 3.5 grams [Wwp = about 3.5 grams], reflecting the marked sexual dimorphism in body size that characterizes this species.

Reproductive output in Triglops nybelini has been quantified under controlled laboratory conditions that closely mimic the species' natural thermal environment. At a stable water temperature of 1.7 °C [T = 1.7 °C], adult females produce an average of 541 eggs per year [Ri = 541 eggs per year], which corresponds to the maximum reproductive rate observed for the species. This annual fecundity value is the principal determinant of the species' daily reproductive output. The demographic implications of this moderate fecundity are interpreted in the context of the species' life-history strategy, which is characterized by relatively slow growth, deferred maturity, and iteroparous spawning over a protracted adult lifespan. The observed reproductive rate is noteworthy when compared to that of other high-latitude cottids, many of which exhibit lower annual fecundities, suggesting that ecological factors such as food availability and predation pressure may have shaped this aspect of the sculpin's reproductive biology.

The early life stages of Bigeye sculpin are defined by a relatively extended period of embryonic development, a consequence of the cold polar waters the species inhabits. The incubation period culminates in eclosion at an age at birth of 133 days [ab = 133 days] post-fertilization, when maintained at the ambient thermal regime of 1.7 °C [T = 1.7 °C]. Newly emerged prolarvae are characterized by a modest wet weight at birth of 0.0035 grams [Wwb = 0.0035 grams], a figure consistent with the small yolk reserves contained within the demersal eggs. These yolk-sac larvae rely on endogenous nutrition during the weeks following chorion rupture, before the onset of exogenous feeding. The protracted incubation period is an adaptation to low metabolic rates at cold temperatures and ensures that larvae emerge during a window of favorable zooplankton abundance, thereby enhancing early feeding success and subsequent survival through the vulnerable pelagic larval phase.

Sexual maturation in Triglops nybelini is a relatively slow process, with individuals reaching the pubertal stage after a considerable post-hatching interval. Under the stable thermal conditions typical of their deep-water Arctic habitat, with water temperatures holding at 1.7 °C [T = 1.7 °C], males and females attain puberty at a time since birth at puberty of approximately 3 years [tp = approximately 3 years]. This deferred onset of reproductive capacity is a characteristic feature of the species' life history and is thought to be driven by the energetic demands of reaching a critical body size, specifically the total length at puberty of 5.6 centimeters [Lp = 5.6 centimeters], before gametogenesis can commence. The lengthy juvenile period allows for the accumulation of sufficient somatic reserves to support the high costs associated with vitellogenesis in females and sperm production in males. This pattern is consistent with the slow life-history pace observed across many Arctic fish species.

Longevity records for Bigeye sculpin indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 7 years [am = approximately 7 years] when individuals are reared under captive conditions at the species' preferred thermal range of 1.7 °C [T = 1.7 °C]. This extended lifespan, coupled with the species' iteroparous reproductive strategy and moderate annual fecundity, suggests a life-history tactic oriented toward the repeated investment in reproduction across multiple seasons. The species' ultimate total length of 14.5 centimeters [Li = 14.5 centimeters] and the corresponding ultimate wet weight for males of 45.9 grams [Wwi = 45.9 grams] represent the peak of somatic investment achieved over this lifespan. Field observations also support this longevity estimate, with recaptured individuals from tagging studies in Greenlandic waters confirming the species' capacity for extended survival and suggesting that senescence-related mortality may be low compared to more short-lived cottid species.
